Rabit:

No offense, @der_andere_Jan, but the last chart (removing the d6s) is pretty biased, […]

None taken
I am aware that this model is very simplistic, and only relates to how strong a background contributes to a character’s strongest suit, in the isolated situation of using a Principle to Overcome without making things worse.
Considering that Principles and their related Overcomes are the defining traits of a character, this doesn’t seem overly far-fetched. Naturally, this is still only a very small piece of what gameplay will entail! I also did not factor in how the following steps of character creation might turn things around; otherwise the math gets quite unwieldy.
It is really only an abstract statistical modelling certainly not covering every situation, but trying to measure the various backgrounds’ starting points against the gist (imho) of a Character’s proficiency, Principle-based Overcomes.

I did not include boost or twists, because they trade success for complication, in that they require spending resources at another point; this moves the imbalance around, but doesn’t negate it.

Simplification aside, I think it still nicely shows that -when it comes to Principle-based Overcomes- the Struggling background contributes very little to begin with, just to illustrate my point that from that point of view, asking for some counter-balancing might be a valid demand (which I had hoped to find inspiration for here).

By the way, another model I had toyed with was die classes, which is not too far from your idea of the sum of averages.
The math is uglier (don’t let me stop you though), but it eventuallly boils down to this:
There are four type of dice available for characters: d6, d8, d10 and d12. Let’s say d6, d8 are the lower class, and d10, d12 are the higher class.
Backgrounds give 5, sometimes 6 dice, and most provide 2 (rarely 3) of those dice in the upper class. Three provide only one in the higher class, instead offering a very constant spread of d8s and nothing below that.
Struggling now not only provides no dice at all in the upper half, it also gives half of its 6 dice at minimum size (d6)!

image631×269 7.73 KB

It’s a little less graphically obvious (and you’ll have to remember no dice can be smaller than d6), but I think the conclusion about Struggling consequently offering lower dice is not really depending on the math model

[…] specifically since one of the benefits of the backgrounds with lower dice is more dice

I would agree that in a more restrictive skill system, having or not having a skill can make a lot of difference - but in SCRPG, where stretching the narrative is the core of the game, I don’t think so much. I personally think that in a game where you can usually pick your dice freely, and where a Quality at “no die” equals a d4, one single d6 makes for a rather poor trade instead of even one single strong die.

I want to throw in my 2 cents.

Overcomes have 100% chance of success without penalties being in play. That too me says that die size does not matter a lot of the time when it comes to Overcomes. Less than 8 on the effect die does result in some sort of twist, but I do not find twist to be completely bad in these circumstances. When a player gets a twist, either from an Overcome or an ability, I like to get the player’s opinion first. I’ll go ahead and use the twist if it works and is better than what I can come up with, meaning twist are as bad or good as the player makes it. I also like narrative twist more so than mechanical twist. This leads me to give a twist that will further a character’s story. If nothing is coming to mind at the time is when I will go ahead and just hand out a penalty or damage.

One example being I have a player whose character had been missing for roughly 10 years. Now their back and have yet to contact any family. A lot of his family’s wealth was spent trying to locate him and they were originally pretty well off. Using a twist one of his siblings is now a thief because they were used to a certain lifestyle. After seeing the player’s character on the news the sibling will track him down and try to use him for his own benefit.

Another character is super into being a hero and likes to check articles to see if he has been noticed. Sometimes when a minor twist shows up I like to use it to say he was accidently left out of all articles related to that event.

How bad of twist are players seeing where they have decided that they must roll an 8?

posts.name: Chaosmancer
posts.cooked:
Well, I haven’t used a lot of twists yet, but damage or penalties is fairly rough. Even min damage can be 3 or more which is 10% of a player’s health.

Also, a penalty can mean that they are more like to get a worse twist the next time, which can spiral.

I’ve also seen between 2 and 8 minions added to a scene because of a twist. This skews the battlefield very much in the villains favor, causing more damage, more hinders, and may slow down achievement of the main goal. Same with Lieutenants, though usually that is just a single lieutenant.

In a similar vein, you can end up with a new overcome challenge, such as civilians in danger or a doomsday plot and that can delay the characters significantly. I actually did use this once and got the people involved a little miffed, because a major twist let to the villain having wired the place to explode, and the characters had to deal with a suddenly much different scene than they were in before, and nearly didn’t make it in time.

You can also lose access to your powers or qualities for an entire session, losing the main way you interact with your character, such as a fire character losing their fire powers is fairly devastating if it happens early on. Great RP potential, but it presents a line that is tricky to deal with.

Yes, twists aren’t bad. Twists can be great and the examples you gave are great uses, but there are also many many uses for twists that can lead to the team getting delayed to the point of failure. Especially if you are triggering twists more often than usual, and end up triggering a spiral.
A character who’s been Struggling their whole life is still in the present unlikely to have an easy time Overcoming things … hm, do tell…
